title: E-Commerce Checkout and Flash Sales
summary: Design cart and checkout for a large online retailer: hold stock, take payment through an external provider and create orders consistently — including flash sales that must never oversell.
statement:
You are designing **cart and checkout for a large online retailer** that sells its own stock from regional warehouses.

**Shoppers**
- Add items to a cart from any device (the cart follows them once they log in; guests have carts too), change quantities and remove items.
- Check out: choose an address, see the final price including discounts, tax and delivery fee, pay, and get an order confirmation.
- Pay by card (sometimes with an extra bank verification step on another page that can take a few minutes), by wallet, or by bank transfer that is confirmed later.
- See hints such as "only 3 left" on product pages, and are told before paying if an item has run out.

**Flash sales**
- Several times a month the retailer runs a flash sale, e.g. 10,000 units of a new phone at a big discount starting at exactly 12:00. Hundreds of thousands of shoppers are waiting on the page and press "Buy" within the first minute. Each shopper may buy at most 1 unit.

**Clarifications from the interviewer**
- A pricing/promotions component that computes a cart's final price and an external payment provider already exist. The provider confirms some payments only later through a webhook, and sometimes times out without saying whether the charge happened.
- Once a shopper starts paying, their items are held for 10 minutes; if payment doesn't complete in time, the items go back on sale.
- After payment, the order is handed to fulfilment (out of scope) through an event.
- A shopper who sees "payment failed" must not have been charged — or must be refunded automatically.

Cover requirements, estimates, APIs, data model and architecture, then dive deep into keeping stock, payments and orders consistent, and into surviving a flash sale.
scaleHints: 20M DAU; ~1M orders/day on normal days (~12/s on average, ~100/s at evening and sale peaks)
~50M cart operations per day (~600/s on average)
Flash sale: ~2M shoppers on the page and ~500K buy attempts in the first 60 s for 10,000 units of one product (~8K attempts/s on a single item)
Checkout API p99 under 1 s excluding time at the payment provider; provider calls take up to 3 s and occasionally time out
Orders retained 7 years for tax purposes (~2 KB per order)
constraints: Never sell more units than are available, including during flash sales
Never charge a shopper twice for one order; every successful charge ends as an order or an automatic refund
Card details are never stored by the retailer (the payment provider tokenises them)
Checkout availability target 99.99%; flash-sale traffic must not take checkout down for regular shoppers
outOfScope: Product search, catalogue browsing and recommendations
Fulfilment, shipping and returns after the order is placed
Pricing/promotions engine and tax calculation internals (given dependencies)
Fraud scoring models and third-party seller features

keyFunctionalRequirements: Cart CRUD for guests and logged-in users, merging carts on login
Checkout: validate the cart, price it via the pricing service, reserve inventory with a 10-minute hold
Payment initiation and confirmation (synchronous and webhook-based) with idempotency
Order creation and state machine (pending payment → paid → sent to fulfilment / cancelled / refunded)
Release holds on timeout or failure; automatic refund when payment succeeds but the order cannot be completed
Flash-sale purchase with a per-user limit and fair, non-overselling allocation
keyNonFunctionalRequirements: Correctness first: no overselling, no double charge, eventual consistency across services backed by reconciliation
Checkout p99 < 1 s excluding provider latency; 99.99% availability
Absorb ~8K attempts/s on a single SKU without collapsing shared databases
Isolation between flash-sale traffic and normal checkout
Auditability and 7-year retention of orders and payment records
coreEntities: Cart: cart_id, user_id/guest_id, items (sku, qty), updated_at
Inventory: sku, warehouse_id, on_hand, reserved, version
Reservation: reservation_id, order_id, sku, qty, status (held/committed/released), expires_at
Order: order_id, user_id, items, amounts, status, idempotency_key, created_at, version
Payment: payment_id, order_id, provider_ref, amount, status (initiated/authorized/captured/failed/unknown/refunded), idempotency_key
Outbox event: event_id, aggregate_id, type, payload, published_at
FlashSale: sale_id, sku, total_units, per_user_limit, start_at; purchase claims per user
keyComponents: Cart service backed by a fast per-user store
Checkout orchestrator (saga) coordinating reservation, payment and order creation with compensations
Inventory service with atomic conditional decrements and expiring holds
Order service owning the order state machine and publishing events through a transactional outbox
Payment service using idempotency keys with the provider, plus webhook handling and status polling
Reconciliation job comparing provider settlement reports with internal payments and orders
Flash-sale admission layer (virtual waiting room / purchase tokens capped at stock) in front of checkout
Hold-expiry worker that releases reserved stock
deepDiveTopics: Inventory holds: row locks vs atomic conditional updates vs pre-split stock buckets for a hot SKU; when to reserve
Saga with compensations instead of distributed transactions; payment that succeeds after the hold expired
Idempotent payments: idempotency keys, unknown outcomes after timeouts, webhooks plus polling, reconciliation
Flash-sale traffic shaping: waiting room, issuing exactly N purchase tokens, per-user limits, protecting downstream services
Transactional outbox for reliably publishing 'order paid' to fulfilment
commonPitfalls: Two-phase commit across inventory, payment and order services
Decrementing stock only after payment (oversell) or at add-to-cart (stock hoarding)
Treating a provider timeout as a failure and letting the shopper pay again
Retrying payment calls without idempotency keys
Letting every flash-sale attempt hit the inventory database row directly
No reconciliation between provider records and internal state
